title: Are AI assisted co-op games an absolute no?
author: tacoteusday1010
selftext:
I’ve been thinking about this lately as I’ve had ideas for games requiring at least 2 players… and I’m curious what other developers think or know about this topic. 

With all the stigma surrounding AI in games, I feel like co-op games might have an even harder time than single-player games.

Here’s my thinking:

**You need multiple people to be on board.** With a single-player game, you only need one person to be interested enough to buy it. But with a co-op game, you need two or more people to agree to play. If even one person in a friend group is strongly against AI, that could be enough to stop the whole group from giving it a chance.

**The more players required, the bigger the problem.** Even if most people don’t really care about AI being used in development, the chances of running into someone who does increase with the number of people needed to play. So a game that requires four players could potentially have a much harder time than one that only requires two.

**Co-op games rely a lot on word of mouth.** A big part of getting people to play these games is having someone convince their friends to buy it too. I wonder if knowing a game was made with AI assistance would make people less likely to recommend it, even if they personally thought it looked fun.

… what do y’all think? I really want to bring some of my ideas to life but don’t want to invest the time and effort if it’s going to be met with extra hate than the usual.

comments.author: BrockFoster
comments.body:
I mean are you going to spend 4 years writing and designing boilerplate stuff when you could streamline the same workflow with one person and accomplish the same thing in less than a year while all the actual heavy lifting into actual design, playability, story, and game logic you wanted to do and spend time on anyways gets all of your attention instead of diluted.

The choice is yours, most of us don’t expect the virtue signaling to last forever

For co-op, sure, you have to get multiple people on board, but players ultimately care if a game is fun and works smoothly with their friends, not whether you used a specific tool to assist in shipping the game

comments.author: Valdaraak
comments.body:
If the game is good, people aren't going to care.

Example: Ark Raiders (AI voices), Crimson Desert (AI art), Call of Duty (AI art. good is subjective, but it's still super popular), Cyberpunk Phantom Liberty (AI voice for Viktor, but also done "ethically"), list goes on and on.

And that's ignoring all the games that use AI code, which is literally every AAA game, including the upcoming GTA6, and most games from smaller studios.

Focus on making a fun game and it won't matter if you used AI.

comments.author: Matilozano96
comments.body:
Edit: reddit mobile lists are buggy as hell lmao…

Forget about the AI usage issue. Coop games are tricky in and of themselves.

1 - Make a good game. First and foremost.

2 - Consider making the game still playable solo (somewhat, at least). Lethal Company isn’t very solo friendly. REPO absolutely is. REPO has a healthier playerbase as a result. (It’s also more polished generally, but the gameplay aspect really sticks out to me). You should try to avoid alienating people who like your game but can't convince a friend to play with them.

3 - Consider non-standard distribution plans for coop. Something to make it very easy to “just try it out” without committing money into it. Steam has support for some things.

Examples:  
To HOST a game, you need a purchase. Joining an existing game is f2p.

Multiplayer Demo with limited gameplay. Let the group test it out before deciding to all buy in.

Buyer gets full features and progression. F2P gets basic ass, boring version with limited progression and no cosmetics.

Etc…
